title: SSH or HTTPS, and why git keeps asking for your password
summary: Switch a remote between URL schemes, rewrite URLs globally with insteadOf, and configure a credential helper so authentication stops being a daily interruption.
mental_model: A remote URL is just config, and git rewrites it through `url.<base>.insteadOf` before using it. Authentication is chosen by scheme: SSH uses your key, HTTPS asks a credential helper. Both are configuration problems, not git problems.

steps.title: See what a remote actually is
steps.why: `remote -v` is a config read. The URL lives in `.git/config` under `remote.<name>.url` — there is no registry and no state beyond that line.
steps.expect: Two remotes, both HTTPS, both plain config entries.

steps.title: Switch one to SSH
steps.why: `remote set-url` rewrites the config line. Nothing else changes — the same commits, the same refs, a different transport and a different way of proving who you are.

steps.title: Rewrite every URL from one host at once
steps.why: `url.<base>.insteadOf` rewrites matching URLs at use time. One config line converts every HTTPS URL for that host to SSH — including ones inside `.gitmodules` that you cannot edit.
steps.expect: The stored URL is still HTTPS, but the URL git would actually use is SSH.

verify.label: the HTTPS URL is rewritten to SSH at use time
…while the config still stores the original URL

steps.title: Fetch over HTTPS, push over SSH
steps.why: `pushInsteadOf` rewrites only push URLs. This is the classic open-source setup: anonymous read over HTTPS with no key needed, authenticated write over SSH.
steps.expect: Fetch resolves to HTTPS, push resolves to SSH — same remote, two URLs.

steps.title: Stop the password prompts
steps.why: Over HTTPS git asks a credential helper for the token. Without one configured it asks you, every time. `store` writes to a plain file, `cache` keeps it in memory, and the platform helpers use the OS keychain — which is the one you want.

steps.title: Configure credentials per host
steps.why: `credential.<url>.*` scopes settings to one host, so a work forge and a personal one can use different usernames and different helpers without interfering.
commands:
sh -c 'printf "protocol=https
host=git.company.example

" | git credential fill --help >/dev/null 2>&1 || true; echo "git credential fill is what git runs internally"'

steps.title: Point a remote at a completely different server
steps.why: Migrations are a config change. Set the new URL, push everything, and every clone that repoints is done — the object database does not care where it came from.
steps.expect: The repository now lives on a different server, with no history change at all.

verify.label: the repository was migrated by changing one config line
verify.hint: git remote set-url origin <new-url>, then push

steps.title: Know which scheme to choose
steps.why: SSH: keys, no prompts, blocked by some corporate firewalls. HTTPS: works everywhere, needs a token and a helper, and is what CI usually uses. Neither is more secure in practice — the difference is operational.
steps.expect: Nothing to run; this step is the summary.

verify.label: pushes to the forge are rewritten to SSH
a credential helper avoids repeated prompts
per-host credential settings are in place
the repository was repointed at a new server successfully

pitfalls: `credential.helper store` writes tokens in plain text to `~/.git-credentials`. Convenient, and a genuine security problem on a shared machine — prefer the OS keychain helper.
`insteadOf` rewrites at use time, so `git remote -v` still shows the original URL. Use `git ls-remote --get-url` to see what git will actually contact.
A helper configured globally applies to every host, including ones you do not control. Scope it with `credential.<url>.helper` when that matters.
Personal access tokens expire. A push that suddenly fails with a 403 after months of working is almost always an expired token, not a permissions change.
SSH host keys change when a forge rotates them, producing an alarming warning. Verify the new fingerprint against the provider's published list before accepting it.
cheatsheet: the URL git will actually use
read over HTTPS, write over SSH
